title: On the Detectability of ChatGPT Content: Benchmarking, Methodology, and Evaluation through the Lens of Academic Writing
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether ChatGPT-generated text can be reliably detected in academic writing, with a particular focus on paper abstracts. The central question is not educational learning outcomes, but the broader detectability of AI-written content in scholarly contexts, including how well humans and existing detectors can distinguish human-written from ChatGPT-written abstracts.

To study this, the authors construct GPABench2, a large benchmark of more than 2.8 million academic abstracts across computer science, physics, and humanities/social sciences. They generate three kinds of ChatGPT outputs: fully written abstracts, completed abstracts, and polished abstracts, using multiple prompt styles. They then evaluate commercial and open-source detectors, build a new detector called CheckGPT, and run a user study with researchers, faculty, and graduate students to test human judgment.

The participants were drawn from a university and a research organization, primarily involving faculty, researchers, and graduate students. The study finds that humans are close to chance at identifying ChatGPT content, even when given examples for reference, and that commercial detectors perform modestly to poorly, especially on polished text. CheckGPT performs very strongly on the benchmark and transfers well across prompts, disciplines, and several external writing datasets, but the paper does not provide evidence about K-12 reading or literacy outcomes.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-based large language model chatbot / text generation system used to compose, complete, and polish text.
identified_tools.use_case: Used to generate academic abstracts in three modes: fully written from scratch, completed from a partial abstract, and polished from an existing abstract. The paper also evaluates GPT-4 on the same abstract-generation tasks as a new source of generated text for detection tests.

quality_tier_rationale: This paper does not evaluate an educational intervention or learner outcome; it is a technical study of detecting ChatGPT-generated academic writing. There is no causal or correlational evidence about K-12 reading/literacy outcomes.
impact_tier_rationale: No reading or literacy outcome is measured, so there is no educational impact on K-12 learners to rate. The reported results concern detectability/classification performance, not student learning.
